question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question:
a. List and explain two privileged actions that an user process may attempt to perform and which
are prevented by the OS via the limited-directed execution setup.
Note that the user process has to know specifically how to make such an attempt.
(e.g., the user process does not know that a PCB exists and hence may not know how to
update its contents).
desired_answer:
- Write to CR3 register to modify page directory pointer
- Write to the EFLAGS registers to modify execution status (zero bit, interrupt enable/disable)
- Write to the IDTR register to change location of IDT
- Access to VA that lies in the kernel virtual address range
student_answer:
1) Creating a new process
Creating a new process using fork() is a privileged action. Creating a new process involves, among many other things, allocating space for a new PCB and populating it. The new process does not know about POS and thus cannot handle its creation on its own and has to request the OS to do so. Furthermore, the OS can prevent the process creation if, say, there is insufficient memory to create a new process.

2) Allocating memory on the heap
Allocating memory on heap (say, by malloc or calloc()) is also a privileged action. It requires finding free physical memory, mapping that memory to physical memory and updating the page table accordingly. The status of the physical memory and the directory of the process is not known by the user process and thus it cannot handle allocating a new page for heap from physical memory. It stays on missing and there needs to request the OS to do so. Furthermore, the OS can prevent the heap expansion if, say, there is insufficient physical memory for the same.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer:
The first system call copies the parent process's
frame into the kernel stack of the child. It
changes the value of the eip register as the
return value of fork() for child is different
from that of the parent. The state of the child
process is set to RUNNABLE. The parent's context is
copied to the child's kernel stack, and then the child
process is returned to back to user-space.

A child process is scheduled by the "context
switch" routine from the kernel. The "call"
is retuned ( has its return value put into the eax
registor) and then passes control back to the
general purpose registers, which returns from the
kernel stack where it was put into by the "fork()"
system call. Then they transfer control to the
process starting entry.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

As part of the fork() syscall implementation,
we copy trapframe of parent to child.
we copy return odds of trap function from parent
stack to child stack.
this ensures that the child will return from trap function
same as that of the parent.
the return addr is instruction next to trap function call
In the syscall function.
-> now it looks like parent, child process called syscall it
is handled as 3
now they are ready to move to user mode
-> once copy of both child, parent are same.
After returning to user mode, depending on
scheduler, both starts executing from the same instruction.

a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

Therefore, when after setting the state of child to RUNNABLE, when child goes to user mode from kernel mode, then it needs to return to return address set at t7 -> eax = forkret() and return to fork() function, from where a it exists in user mode and then it is scheduled via sched().

a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer: When a fork() system call is made, it does two main things. First, it sets the return value to zero for the newly created child process. It also copies the trapframe of the process that created the child process to the newly created child's trapframe. Second, it makes the trapframe PC point to a special function called folk_det(). So, when a newly created child is scheduled for the first time, it first goes to folk_set() function. In this function, the child processes will return to the user mode from the kernel mode.

the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).

Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

Since the child process is (almost) related to the parent
the RIGHT trap of the parent is captured to the 
child (except eax which is copied to the 
the child & ebx for parent). The return value is 0 (zero)
another schedulable entity & when it is 
scheduled by the scheduler the OS via the trapframe of the
process knows that it had to return to the process
via the interrupt handler, it also uses the topframe
to infer where in the process it had to return to.

the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer:
The fork() system call was called inside parent, but both parent and child return from fork as two separate processes.
fork creates a trap frame for the child process and puts return value as 0 in it. This happens because fork behaves as follows:
1. identical FCB (except pid) and virtual address space.
2. fork() , after creating the new process, puts return value 0 in the stack of the child process. Therefore, when child process is scheduled, it behaves as if it has just returned from trap with return value as 0. (fork with a new trap frame)
3. Then stk() returns child's pid for parent as usual.

5 steps:
1. stk
2. child obj
3. fork copies this form parent VA space.
4. 0'
5. return value

parent VA   child VA
Therefore, child and parent are identical except pid and return addresses of fork.

process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).

Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer:
The trap/interrupt handler is not something specific to a process, but a property of the OS. So a child process also has the same trap/interrupt handlers as the parent process.
It returns from kernel mode to the user mode, and returns using the same return path as the parent called.
But if we're talking about how one child process returns from kernel mode (when invoked by a fork()), then it is a bit tricky, since the child process was just created and it doesn't make a system call on any other trap, so it's return path will also change.

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)

and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).

the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

The fork system call sets the value of eax register (return value) in the stackframe of the child process to 0.

the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer: When allocating/creating a new process on the fork system calls the kernel Stack and trap frame of the parent process is copied to that of the child process. The only field which is not copied is the register which stores the return value of the system call (eax). For the parent process, the pid of the child process is returned and for the child process the value 0 is returned. What is noteworthy is that both the parent process and the child process store the same value in the eip registers which stores the value of the program counter or the instruction pointer. Hence, even the child process returns from a trap since the trap instruction was getting handled be right before its creation

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer:
Solution: When fork is called, all the stack heap and other data variables of the process are copied into a new stack/memory space with a different pid number.
When executing the child process, all the data variables are stored in the kernel stack and when the process is done the data is copied into the original stack and the return values are stored in trap table, the child process then calls the parent to execute.

good_answer: - When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode. Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode. - The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function (e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret) - As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address). - This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer: When a fork() system call is made, it copies all the contents of the PCB of the parent-process to the PCB of the child process. PCB stores the information about trapframe also (address of the trapframe contents in the stack). The system call not just copies the contents of trapframe of parent-process to that in the child process, it also creates a new trapframe for the child process and copies the contents of trapframe of parent-process to that in the child process. This trapframe shows information about the trap including the return address. Thus the trap-handler utilizes the trapframe to make the child process return from a trap even though there was no trap in the child process.

Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode. - The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function (e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret) - As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address). - This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
desired_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
student_answer:
When we fork a process in kernel mode we create a new process allocate pagetables open files, etc which are same as it's parent. Then we allocate a new page for kernel stack of new process and additionally copy trapframe of parent in trap frame of child. So we change eax value in new process and call trap which will pop all registers put in trapframe by alltraps. Then subsequently "iret" which will pop first register corresponding to user state in program like eip, cs, eflags, and change privilege mode and return to user process.

np                       s2 + STACKSIZE - size_of(np->tf);   //np->new process
copy(p, &parent->np->tf);
np->tf.eax = 0;
trapret;    //pop all general purpose registers
iret;       //pop all user stack
